title: What do people make their AI do?
summary: An explorer of 16,591 public instruction files that developers write for their AI agents.
problem: People now write instruction files (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md) that tell AI agents what to do and what never to do. There are around two million of them on GitHub, and nobody had looked at what they actually say. I wanted to know for my master's thesis on how AI agents change the way work is organised.
built: A small pipeline that searches GitHub, downloads the files, and sorts every one by what it hands to the AI, which rules it sets and what it forbids. Claude read a random sample of 100 to check the keyword sorting. On top sits an interactive page with a constellation of what goes together and click-through quotes from real files.
result: 16,591 files analysed in an afternoon. Testing (59%) and coding (53%) are what people hand over most; not committing or pushing without permission is the most common ban. The pilot also showed that word counting misses most rules, which shapes the method for the thesis.

title: AlphaCRM: accounting integrations
summary: Connected Alpha's CRM to the three accounting systems Danish small businesses use most.
problem: AlphaCRM is a CRM that the customer owns outright, with no subscription. Danish small businesses keep their books in e-conomic, Billy or Dinero, and a CRM that cannot talk to the books is a hard sell.
built: Integrations with e-conomic, Billy and Dinero, so customers and invoices move between the CRM and the accounting system.
result: The work was estimated at 44 to 64 hours. Building with AI, it took about 5.

title: AlphaCRM in English
summary: An English version of the CRM, with a language switcher, so it can sell beyond Denmark.
problem: The CRM was Danish only, which closed the door to customers outside Denmark and to Alpha's international team.
built: Translated the interface and added language switching across the app.
result: The product can now be shown and sold in English.

title: AlphaCRM help site and guide videos
summary: A searchable help site with a narrated video for every guide.
problem: A new customer meets the product alone, weeks after signing. Help built into each installation is hard to keep up to date.
built: A standalone help site with written guides, search across everything, a catalogue of add-ons, and five guide videos with voiceover, generated from code so they can be re-rendered when the product changes.
result: One place to fix a guide instead of every installation, and videos that can be remade in minutes instead of re-recorded.

title: Interactive sales presentation
summary: A web-based sales deck for the CRM that the sales lead can edit himself.
problem: Slides go stale and every edit had to go through the person who made them.
built: A presentation that runs in the browser, with an edit mode so the sales lead can change the wording himself. It is linked from the company's internal system.
result: Used in sales meetings and kept current by the people who use it.

title: Lead forms and pages on the agency website
summary: Landing pages, lead forms and the CRM product pages on the agency's own site, in Danish, English and Swedish.
problem: The website is where leads arrive, and the forms decide what lands in the email system afterwards. Broken phone numbers or missing consent make a lead useless.
built: Landing pages for a split test between two wordings, lead forms with an industry dropdown, phone numbers cleaned into one format and a proper consent checkbox, an add-ons section on the CRM page in three languages, and contact forms on the case pages.
result: Live on the agency's site. Leads now arrive clean, with consent recorded, straight into the email system.

title: Sales deck hub
summary: One place for every sales deck, which the salespeople can edit themselves without asking anyone.
problem: Sales decks lived as files that went out of date, and every change had to go through the person who made them.
built: A small site that lists every sales deck. Each deck runs in the browser, and adding ?rediger to its address opens an edit mode, so the salespeople update the text themselves. Linked from the company's internal system.
result: Used by the sales team in customer meetings and kept current by the people who present them.

title: AlphaCRM guided product tour
summary: A clickable demo of the CRM with a step-by-step tour, so prospects can try it before a meeting.
problem: A prospect could not try the CRM without a meeting, and an empty system says little on its own.
built: A public demo version of the CRM with no real data, a ten-step guided tour of the menu, and a getting-started checklist that shows a new customer what to do first.
result: Live and open to anyone. Try it yourself.

title: AI post generators for a franchise and a clinic
summary: AI tools that draft on-brand social posts for every branch of a franchise, and for a chiropractic clinic, with a person approving each one.
problem: Local businesses need regular, on-brand posts. Writing them by hand does not scale, a designer opening Illustrator for every post is slow, and fully automatic posting is a risk.
built: For a franchise with many branches: a generator inside the agency's social media platform that drafts posts and images for each branch, with a review queue where a person approves, edits or rejects each one, filled by scheduled agents over the weekend. For a chiropractic clinic: a web tool where the team picks one of the designer's templates, gets AI-suggested text with a named source for every figure, swaps the photo and downloads a finished post in minutes.
result: Posts are ready for review every Monday, and a clinic post that used to need a designer now takes a few minutes. A person still approves everything before it goes out.

title: Tyre advice chat agent
summary: One chat agent for a tyre chain's website that advises customers and sends them to a dealer that is open.
problem: The first idea was one agent per dealer website. A check showed almost no dealers had their own site, so the real job was one agent on the chain's site covering all of them.
built: An AI chat agent that gives tyre advice using only the chain's own pages, sends the customer to the nearest dealer that is actually open, and hands over to booking.
result: Built and deployed in a single working shift.

title: Agents that work the weekend
summary: Scheduled AI agents that check, draft and prepare work while the office is closed.
problem: Routine checks and drafts eat into the working week.
built: Cloud agents on a schedule: one checks the email programme every Saturday, one fills the social post queue, one finds content ideas and emails them to the content team on Sunday.
result: The team starts Monday with checks done and drafts waiting, and a person still decides what ships.

title: Email programme for a jewellery brand
summary: Audit, welcome series, abandoned cart and win-back emails for a Danish jewellery webshop.
problem: The brand had Klaviyo but little running in it, and the emails that existed did not look or sound like the brand.
built: An audit with a proposal, then a three-email welcome series, an abandoned cart email and two win-back campaigns, written in the brand's voice and styled in its own palette. The client chose the final colours from a clickable PDF of six variants.
result: The audit turned into a proposal for an ongoing hours package, and the emails were reworked from the client's own feedback.

title: Email for Alpha's own AI brand
summary: Fixed consent, built a welcome flow and a monthly newsletter, with an agent that checks it weekly.
problem: The sign-up forms did not collect consent the way Danish marketing law requires, and there was no newsletter.
built: Consent fixes on every form, a welcome flow, a monthly newsletter format and a house style guide for emails. An AI agent reviews the whole programme every weekend and reports what needs fixing.
result: Compliant sign-ups and a newsletter that runs on a routine.

title: Creative pre-flight tool
summary: Lets a designer see her ads inside real Meta and Google placements, and flags problems before handover.
problem: The agency's designer had no access to the ad platforms, so she never saw her designs live. Text hidden under platform buttons, covers cropped differently on mobile and white text on light backgrounds only surfaced after handover.
built: A browser tool: drop in finished designs and see them in realistic ad mock-ups on phone and desktop, with automatic format and readability checks. The format specs were verified against the platforms' own documentation, and the files never leave the browser.
result: Problems are caught by the designer herself, before the files reach marketing.

title: Thai learning app
summary: My own app for learning Thai beyond the conversational level.
problem: I speak conversational Thai and want to read and write it properly, but most apps stop at tourist phrases.
built: A personal learning app built around the words and phrases I actually meet at work and in daily life, with tone practice and an AI tutor.
result: My own practice tool, built in a day from a long spec.

title: Research journal on an AI-first agency
summary: 150+ field notes on how a small AI-first agency really works, for my internship report and thesis.
problem: My master's programme asks for research based on the internship. Memory is not data.
built: A structured research journal: field notes filed during the working day, coded with the Gioia method, with weekly summaries and an AI that argues against my research questions.
result: The evidence base for my internship report and the starting point for my thesis.

title: Master's thesis: A team of one?
summary: How AI agents change the way work is organised, and whether one person with agents can do what used to take a team.
problem: A common claim is that one person working with AI agents can now do work that used to need a team. It is repeated a lot and researched very little.
built: A thesis for my MSc in Innovation Management (University of Chinese Academy of Sciences and Aalborg University), using public instruction files that people write for their AI agents and a questionnaire, framed with organisation theory on why teams and firms exist.
result: In progress, due June 2027. The agent files explorer is the pilot for its data.

title: Internship research report
summary: A research report on how work changes when AI takes over producing a classic agency service.
problem: My master's programme asks for a research report built on the internship, tied to tasks I actually did.
built: A study of an AI-driven social media and email service at an AI-first agency, based on my own research journal of field notes and the work records of the tasks.
result: Due January 2027.

title: Pharma flu logistics optimizer, with Moonshot AI
summary: Digital Innovation course, group project in collaboration with Moonshot AI, the company behind Kimi: a control-tower app that helps a pharmaceutical warehouse plan for flu season.
problem: Flu outbreaks make demand for medicine jump suddenly and unevenly across regions. A central warehouse that plans for a normal week ends up short-staffed, behind on next-day delivery and mixing cold-chain goods badly.
built: A Python app built together with Kimi, Moonshot AI's model, with five pages: a dashboard comparing Normal, Peak and Flu Season scenarios; wave planning that groups orders with machine-learning clustering and keeps room-temperature, cold and frozen goods apart; a what-if simulator; a manager overview with KPIs; and a dictionary of terms. It scores flu risk for eight regions from public health data and forecasts demand per product for 7, 30 and 90 days. We used AI for the code and added the pharma business rules ourselves.
result: Presented at the course's Final Demo Day on 10 June 2026. It now runs entirely in the browser; the first visit takes about a minute while Python loads.

title: How Danish life science firms adapt in China
summary: Semester 2 group project, MSc Innovation Management: how Danish life science companies changed their view of China from 2021 to 2025, and how they adapt their business models.
problem: Danish life science is one of the country's biggest exports, and China is a key market. Since 2021, geopolitical tension and a growing gap between headquarters in Denmark and the teams in China have made the old growth plans hard to follow.
built: A mixed-methods study: five years of the Danish Business Outlook on China survey data analysed over time, plus interviews with business organisations and managers at two major Danish life science companies. Framed with business model innovation, activity systems, dynamic capabilities and horizon scanning.
result: Sentiment went from optimism in 2021, through a sharp fall in 2022, to a neutral level by 2024-25. Firms are moving from a headquarters-led growth model to a more local, risk-aware one: local activities and talent, new partnerships and digital channels. The conclusion: adapting is a continuous reconfiguration, not a one-time strategy change.

title: Bringing Chinese consumer electronics to Denmark
summary: Semester 1 group project (team Triple Helix): a market-entry framework for a Danish design and trading company scouting Chinese gadgets for the Nordic market.
problem: China leads in new consumer electronics, but products that succeed there often fail in Denmark because of different habits, regulation and trust expectations. The company needed a structured way to pick winners.
built: A scouting and evaluation framework built on Rogers' diffusion of innovations, the Lean Startup and Blue Ocean Strategy, tested with a focus group and a survey of 41 Danish consumers on three candidate products.
result: Danish consumers are open to new products but adopt cautiously: trust, quality and everyday usefulness matter more than novelty or the country of origin. A UV toothbrush sterilizer showed the strongest potential, a handheld steamer suited early adopters, and an indoor hydroponic garden would need simplifying first.
